claim: The ER membrane protein complex (EMC) was first described in yeast as a complex of 6 co-purifying and conserved proteins (Emc1-6) with strongly correlated phenotypes in a double mutant genetic modifier map of the unfolded protein response.
source: The EMC was first described in yeast as a complex of 6 co-purifying and conserved proteins (Emc1-6) with strongly correlated phenotypes in a double mutant genetic modifier map of the unfolded protein response (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jonikas et al., 2009, which is the original study describing the EMC complex.

claim: The pattern of EMC genetic interactions strongly resembles the pattern of other factors whose loss leads to the accumulation of misfolded membrane proteins.
source: The pattern of EMC genetic interactions strongly resembles the pattern of other factors whose loss leads to the accumulation of misfolded membrane proteins, including the overexpression of a misfolded membrane protein (Sec61-2), and these insights first suggested that the EMC may be a TMD protein chaperone (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jonikas et al., 2009, which provided genetic interaction data suggesting the EMC's role in membrane protein folding.

claim: The mammalian EMC orthologues were identified in a mammalian physical interaction map of ER-associated degradation (ERAD) components.
source: The mammalian EMC orthologues were subsequently identified in a mammalian physical interaction map of ER-associated degradation (ERAD) components (Christianson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Christianson et al., 2011, which identified mammalian EMC components.

claim: Loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of specific multipass membrane proteins in S. cerevisiae (a Yor1 mutant which mimicked a common disease allele of CFTR, and Mrh1).
source: In vivo experiments have shown that loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of specific multipass membrane proteins in S. cerevisiae (a Yor1 mutant which mimicked a common disease allele of CFTR, and Mrh1) (Louie et al., 2012; Bircham et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Louie et al., 2012 and Bircham et al., 2011, which demonstrated EMC's role in specific membrane protein biogenesis in yeast.

claim: Loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of rhodopsin in D. melanogaster.
source: In vivo experiments have shown that loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of specific multipass membrane proteins in S. cerevisiae (a Yor1 mutant which mimicked a common disease allele of CFTR, and Mrh1) (Louie et al., 2012; Bircham et al., 2011), D. melanogoster (rhodopsin) (Satoh et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Satoh et al., 2015, which showed EMC's role in rhodopsin biogenesis in Drosophila.

claim: Loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of acetylcholine receptors in C. elegans.
source: In vivo experiments have shown that loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of specific multipass membrane proteins in S. cerevisiae (a Yor1 mutant which mimicked a common disease allele of CFTR, and Mrh1) (Louie et al., 2012; Bircham et al., 2011), D. melanogoster (rhodopsin) (Satoh et al., 2015), C. elegans (acetylcholine receptors) (Richard et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Richard et al., 2013, which demonstrated EMC's role in acetylcholine receptor biogenesis in C. elegans.

claim: Loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of ABCA3 in mice.
source: In vivo experiments have shown that loss of the EMC compromises synthesis, stabilization and/or trafficking of specific multipass membrane proteins in S. cerevisiae (a Yor1 mutant which mimicked a common disease allele of CFTR, and Mrh1) (Louie et al., 2012; Bircham et al., 2011), D. melanogoster (rhodopsin) (Satoh et al., 2015), C. elegans (acetylcholine receptors) (Richard et al., 2013) and mice (ABCA3) (Tang et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2017, which showed EMC's role in ABCA3 biogenesis in mice.

claim: Knockdown of an EMC component compromised biogenesis of mutant CFTR expressed in HeLa cells.
source: and that knockdown of an EMC component compromised biogenesis of mutant CFTR expressed in HeLa cells (Louie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Louie et al., 2012, which demonstrated EMC's role in CFTR biogenesis in mammalian cells.

claim: The EMC has been implicated in autophagy.
source: In addition, the EMC has been implicated in autophagy (Shen et al., 2016; Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shen et al., 2016 and Li et al., 2013, which implicated EMC in autophagy.

claim: The EMC has been implicated in lipid transfer and tethering between the ER and mitochondria.
source: In addition, the EMC has been implicated in autophagy (Shen et al., 2016; Li et al., 2013), lipid transfer and tethering between the ER and mitochondria (Lahiri et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lahiri et al., 2014, which implicated EMC in ER-mitochondria interactions.

claim: The EMC has been implicated in flavivirus replication.
source: and flavivirus replication (Zhang et al., 2016; Savidis et al., 2016; Marceau et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2015; Krishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Zhang et al., 2016; Savidis et al., 2016; Marceau et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2015; Krishnan et al., 2008) that implicated EMC in flavivirus replication.

claim: The EMC acts as a posttranslational insertase into the ER membrane for the sterol biosynthesis enzyme, squalene synthase (SQS/FDFT1) and a subset of other tail-anchored (TA) proteins.
source: Finally, the EMC was recently shown to act as a posttranslational insertase into the ER membrane for the sterol biosynthesis enzyme, squalene synthase (SQS/FDFT1) and a subset of other tail-anchored (TA) proteins.
evidence: This claim is stated as a recent finding in the manuscript, referring to the EMC's role as a TA protein insertase.

claim: EMC TA substrates have moderately hydrophobic TMDs rendering them unable to interact with TRC40/Get3, the cytosolic receptor that delivers TA proteins to the dominant ER insertase, GET1/2.
source: These TA substrates have moderately hydrophobic TMDs rendering them unable to interact with TRC40/Get3, the cytosolic receptor that delivers TA proteins to the dominant ER insertase, GET1/2 (24).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (24) describing the properties of EMC TA substrates and their inability to use the TRC40/Get3 pathway.

claim: Emc3 interacts with roughly stoichiometric quantities of all core EMC components (Emc1, Emc2, Emc4, Emc5 and Emc6) and the accessory proteins Sop4 and Emc10.
source: As expected, we identified roughly stoichiometric quantities of all core EMC components (Emc1, Emc2, Emc4, Emc5 and Emc6) and the accessory proteins Sop4 and Emc10 (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from Emc3-3xFLAG pulldowns, with reference to Jonikas et al., 2009 for the identification of EMC components.

claim: Emc3 interacts with several large, multi-pass membrane proteins (Pma1, Fks1, Spf1) and Ilm1.
source: In addition to EMC components, Emc3 interacted with several large, multi-pass membrane proteins (Pma1, Fks1, Spf1) and Ilm1, a poorly characterized ER-localized protein (Lockshon et al., 2007) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from Emc3-3xFLAG pulldowns shown in Figure 1A, with a citation to Lockshon et al., 2007 for Ilm1 localization.

claim: SILAC analysis verified specific interactions between the EMC and multipass membrane proteins (Spf1, Fks1, and Pma1) and Ilm1.
source: This quantitative analysis verified interactions with all core (Emc1-6) and accessory EMC components (Sop4 and Emc10), and demonstrated specific interactions between the EMC, multipass membrane proteins (Spf1, Fks1, and Pma1) and Ilm1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative SILAC mass spectrometry data comparing Emc3-3xFLAG and Orm1-3xFLAG pulldowns, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The EMC specifically interacts with Erg9, the yeast homolog of a TA protein recently shown to be inserted into the ER in an EMC-dependent manner.
source: We also detected specific interaction with Erg9, the yeast homolog of a TA protein recently shown to be inserted into the ER in an EMC-dependent manner (Guna et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data detecting Erg9 interaction with EMC, with a citation to Guna et al., 2018 for the EMC-dependent insertion of this TA protein.

claim: Sop4 is a specialized chaperone/transport factor required for the biogenesis of the yeast plasma membrane ATPase (Pma1).
source: Sop4 was previously shown to be a specialized chaperone/transport factor required for the biogenesis of the yeast plasma membrane ATPase (Pma1), (Luo et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2002, which demonstrated Sop4's role as a Pma1 chaperone.

claim: Gsf2 plays a role in the biogenesis and export of hexose transporter 1 (Hxt1) from the ER.
source: and Gsf2 plays a role in the biogenesis and export of hexose transporter 1 (Hxt1) from the ER (Sherwood and Carlson, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sherwood and Carlson, 1999, which demonstrated Gsf2's role in Hxt1 biogenesis.

claim: ILM1 deletion results in enhanced oleic acid sensitivity, likely due to a cell wall defect.
source: ILM1 deletion results in enhanced oleic acid sensitivity, likely due to a cell wall defect (Lockshon et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lockshon et al., 2007, which reported the oleic acid sensitivity phenotype of ILM1 deletion.

claim: ILM1 deletion showed increased sensitivity to caspofungin, similar to the deletion phenotype for FKS1.
source: and showed increased sensitivity to caspofungin, similar to the deletion phenotype for FKS1 (Markovich et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Markovich et al., 2004, which reported the caspofungin sensitivity phenotype of FKS1 deletion, and implies comparison with ILM1 deletion.

claim: Ilm1 shows a near stoichiometric interaction with Fks1.
source: We observed a near stoichiometric interaction between Ilm1 and Fks1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from Ilm1-3xFLAG pulldowns shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ilm1 interacts with components of the EMC (Emc1 and Emc2), ER oxidoreductase 1 (Ero1) and general chaperone proteins (Ssa1, Ssb1 and Kar2).
source: Other prominent bands were identified as components of the EMC (Emc1 and Emc2), ER oxidoreductase 1 (Ero1) and general chaperone proteins (Ssa1, Ssb1 and Kar2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from Ilm1-3xFLAG pulldowns identifying these interacting proteins.

claim: FKS1 deletion results in hypersensitivity to compounds, such as calcofluor white, that affect cell wall assembly.
source: As the catalytic subunit of the 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase cell wall biosynthesis enzyme, FKS1 deletion results in hypersensitivity to compounds, such as calcofluor white, that affect cell wall assembly (Ram et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ram et al., 1995, which reported the calcofluor white sensitivity phenotype of FKS1 deletion.

claim: The ∆ilm1 strain shows profound sensitivity to calcofluor white with growth decreased at 3 µg/ml and completely inhibited at 6 µg/ml.
source: Indeed, we found profound sensitivity with growth decreased at 3 µg/ml and completely inhibited at 6 µg/ml calcofluor white in the ∆ilm1 background (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing calcofluor white sensitivity of ∆ilm1 strain, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ∆emc2 strain shows increased sensitivity to calcofluor white at 6 µg/ml compared to wild type.
source: We also noted increased sensitivity compared to wild type for ∆emc2 at 6 µg/ml, further supporting a role for the EMC in maintaining cell wall integrity, possibly by promoting the biosynthesis of Fks1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing calcofluor white sensitivity of ∆emc2 strain, with inference about EMC's role in cell wall integrity.

claim: Deletion of Ilm1 results in a prominent increase in EMC association with Fks1 and the functionally redundant paralog, Gsc2.
source: Rather than a decrease in the interaction between the EMC and multipass proteins, as predicted by the bridging model, we observed a prominent increase in EMC association with Fks1 and the functionally redundant paralog, Gsc2, in the ∆ilm1 background
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data comparing EMC3-3xFlag interactions in wild type and ∆ilm1 strains.

claim: Deletion of Sop4 results in increased EMC association with Elo2, Pma1 and Mrh1.
source: as well as Elo2, Pma1 and Mrh1 in the ∆sop4 background (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data comparing EMC3-3xFlag interactions in wild type and ∆sop4 strains, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mrh1 was previously shown to be dependent on the EMC for its biosynthesis and cell surface localization.
source: Interestingly, Mrh1 was previously shown to be dependent on the EMC for its biosynthesis and cell surface localization (Bircham et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bircham et al., 2011, which demonstrated EMC's role in Mrh1 biogenesis.

claim: Deletion of Ilm1 or Sop4 results in a decrease in general chaperone proteins (Ssa1, Ssb1, and Kar2) associated with EMC3-3xFLAG.
source: Consistent with a role for Ilm1 and Sop4 as membrane protein-specific chaperones, we observed a decrease in general chaperone proteins (Ssa1, Ssb1, and Kar2) and an increase in ribosomal proteins associated with EMC3-3xFLAG in strains missing these factors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data comparing EMC3-3xFlag interactions in wild type, ∆ilm1, and ∆sop4 strains, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of Ilm1 or Sop4 results in an increase in ribosomal proteins associated with EMC3-3xFLAG.
source: Consistent with a role for Ilm1 and Sop4 as membrane protein-specific chaperones, we observed a decrease in general chaperone proteins (Ssa1, Ssb1, and Kar2) and an increase in ribosomal proteins associated with EMC3-3xFLAG in strains missing these factors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data comparing EMC3-3xFlag interactions in wild type, ∆ilm1, and ∆sop4 strains, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The EMC interacts with multipass membrane proteins transiting through the ER, membrane protein specific co-chaperones, general chaperones, and the ribosome.
source: Together, these pulldown experiments showed that the EMC interacts with multipass membrane proteins transiting through the ER, membrane protein specific co-chaperones, general chaperones, and the ribosome.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the pulldown experiments described in Figures 1 and 2, supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The presence of client-specific co-chaperones (Ilm1 and Sop4) enhances the interaction between the EMC and general chaperones and decreases the association with both multipass transmembrane clients and the ribosome.
source: The presence of client-specific co-chaperones (Ilm1 and Sop4) enhances the interaction between the EMC and general chaperones and decreases the association with both multipass transmembrane clients and the ribosome (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data comparing EMC interactions in the presence and absence of Ilm1 and Sop4, summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: The EMC interacts directly with multipass transmembrane client proteins early during their synthesis, insertion or folding independent of and possibly prior to chaperone engagement.
source: These observations suggest that the EMC interacts directly with multipass transmembrane client proteins early during their synthesis, insertion or folding independent of and possibly prior to chaperone engagement.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that deletion of co-chaperones increases EMC-client interactions and decreases EMC-chaperone interactions.

claim: The profile of the ratio of pulldown-to-total footprint reads across FKS1 and GSC2 revealed prominent increases in EMC-ribosome proximity immediately following the translation of clusters of TMDs.
source: The profile of this ratio across FKS1 and GSC2 revealed prominent increases in EMC-ribosome proximity immediately following the translation of clusters of TMDs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-specific ribosome profiling data for FKS1 and GSC2, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The enrichment pattern for FKS1 and GSC2 was not observed in strains with two other ER-localized BirA fusions (BirA-Ubc6-TA and BirA-Ssh1).
source: This enrichment pattern was not observed in strains with two other ER-localized BirA fusions (BirA-Ubc6-TA and BirA-Ssh1), suggesting that the EMC specifically interacts with these nascent chains shortly after synthesis of TMD clusters by the ribosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-specific ribosome profiling data comparing Emc5-BirA with BirA-Ubc6-TA and BirA-Ssh1, demonstrating specificity of EMC engagement.

claim: 51 genes reproducibly showed localized peaks of Emc5-specific enrichment (defined as being in the top 10% of eligible genes in each of two biological replicates).
source: In addition to the most enriched genes (FKS1 and GSC2), we identified 51 genes that reproducibly showed localized peaks of Emc5-specific enrichment (defined as being in the top 10% of eligible genes in each of two biological replicates; see Materials and methods) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic analysis of proximity-specific ribosome profiling data, with the list of 51 genes shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The list of putative EMC client proteins includes two genes for which the EMC was previously implicated in their biogenesis (PMA1 and YOR1).
source: This list of putative EMC client proteins includes two genes for which the EMC was previously implicated in their biogenesis (PMA1 and YOR1) (Louie et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-specific ribosome profiling data identifying PMA1 and YOR1 as EMC clients, with citations to Louie et al., 2012 and Luo et al., 2002 for previous evidence of EMC involvement.

claim: Emc5-BirA positional enrichment for client proteins typically was triggered following synthesis of a cluster of TMDs.
source: Emc5-BirA positional enrichment for client proteins typically was triggered following synthesis of a cluster of TMDs (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of proximity-specific ribosome profiling data for EMC clients, with detailed data in Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: For Emc5-BirA, the EMC clients showed a continued increase in enrichment such that the maximum was achieved following synthesis of an additional ~100 amino acids after the first TMD.
source: By contrast, for Emc5-BirA, the EMC clients, but not the full set of TMDs, showed a continued increase in enrichment such that the maximum was achieved following synthesis of an additional ~100 amino acids.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of average enrichments around the first TMD for EMC clients compared to all TMD-containing proteins.

claim: The full list of EMC clients was strongly enriched for multipass proteins.
source: Strikingly, the full list of EMC clients was strongly enriched for multipass proteins (Figure 4A)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the number of TMDs in EMC clients compared to all secretory proteins, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EMC-interacting TMDs were enriched for charged amino acids and depleted for hydrophobic amino acids, including aliphatic residues common in TMDs.
source: and EMC-interacting TMDs were enriched for charged amino acids and depleted for hydrophobic amino acids, including aliphatic residues common in TMDs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by amino acid composition analysis of TMDs in EMC clients compared to all TMDs, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gene ontology term enrichment on the set of putative EMC clients showed enrichment for terms related to transporters.
source: Gene ontology term enrichment on the set of putative EMC clients showed enrichment for terms related to transporters; indeed, a majority of clients are classified as transporters (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of EMC clients, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Integral membrane glycosyltransferases, including beta-glucan synthase genes (FSK1 and GSC2) defined a second class of putative EMC clients.
source: Notably, integral membrane glycosyltransferases (which must overcome the challenge of transferring hydrophilic sugars onto membrane-associated substrates), including beta-glucan synthase genes (FSK1 and GSC2) defined a second class of putative EMC clients (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of EMC clients, shown in Figure 4C, with inference about the functional challenges these proteins face.

claim: EMC2 depletion affects the abundance of all detected members of the EMC complex.
source: Whereas EMC2 depletion affects the abundance of all detected members of the EMC complex, depletion of EMC4 has no effect on other EMC members (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data comparing EMC2 and EMC4 depletion, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Depletion of EMC4 has no effect on other EMC members.
source: Whereas EMC2 depletion affects the abundance of all detected members of the EMC complex, depletion of EMC4 has no effect on other EMC members (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data comparing EMC2 and EMC4 depletion, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: EMC2 but not EMC4 is structurally integral to the formation of the EMC complex.
source: We thus infer that EMC2 but not EMC4 is structurally integral to the formation of the EMC complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that EMC2 depletion affects all EMC members while EMC4 depletion does not.

claim: Proteomic changes in EMC2 and EMC4 knockdown cell lines were strongly correlated, except for EMC components.
source: Proteomic changes in these two EMC-depleted cell lines were measured against a control cell line expressing a non-targeting guide RNA (GAL4). Except for EMC components, almost all observed changes were strongly correlated between the EMC2 and EMC4 knockdown cell lines (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data comparing EMC2 and EMC4 depletion, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The translation rate of the vast majority of potential client proteins is unaffected by EMC2 depletion, with the notable exception of ATP6V0A1.
source: This analysis revealed that the translation rate of the vast majority of potential client proteins is unaffected (with the notable exception of ATP6V0A1, which is decreased at both the translational and protein level), consistent with post-translational degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data comparing translation rates in EMC2-depleted and control cells, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Proteins that are upregulated at the protein level in EMC-depleted cells are also upregulated at the translational level, indicating transcriptional and/or translational induction.
source: By contrast, proteins that are upregulated at the protein level are also upregulated at the translational level, indicating transcriptional and/or translational induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ribosome profiling and proteomics data in EMC-depleted cells, with inference about the mechanism of upregulation.

claim: Proteins upregulated at the translatome and proteome-level in EMC-depleted cells are enriched for gene ontology terms related to the unfolded protein response.
source: As expected from EMC genetic interactions, 2D annotation enrichment (Cox and Mann, 2012) shows that proteins upregulated at the translatome and proteome-level are enriched for gene ontology terms related to the unfolded protein response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Jonikas et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D annotation enrichment analysis of proteins upregulated in EMC-depleted cells, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, with citations to Cox and Mann, 2012 for the method and Jonikas et al., 2009 for EMC genetic interactions.

claim: Analysis of the proteins degraded upon EMC-depletion reveals an enrichment for proteins that enter the secretory pathway.
source: By contrast, analysis of the proteins degraded upon EMC-depletion reveals an enrichment for proteins that enter the secretory pathway (Supplementary File 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of proteins decreased in EMC-depleted cells, with detailed data in Supplementary File 1.

claim: Of the 11 proteins decreased by 2-fold or more in both EMC2- and EMC4-depleted cells, 10 have at least one transmembrane domain.
source: Moreover, of the 11 proteins decreased by 2-fold or more in both EMC2- and EMC4-depleted cells, 10 have at least one transmembrane domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of proteins significantly decreased in EMC-depleted cells.

claim: The levels of mammalian squalene synthase (FDFT1) and TREX1 decreased upon EMC depletion, confirming a role for the EMC in TA protein insertion.
source: Confirming a role for the EMC in TA protein insertion (Guna et al., 2012018), the levels of mammalian squalene synthase (FDFT1) and TREX1 (35) decreased upon EMC depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data showing decreased levels of FDFT1 and TREX1 in EMC-depleted cells, with a citation to Guna et al., 2018 for the EMC's role in TA protein insertion.

claim: The cohort of putative EMC client proteins in human cells is strongly enriched for multipass transmembrane proteins.
source: However, similar to that seen in yeast, the cohort of putative EMC client proteins is strongly enriched for multipass transmembrane proteins (Figure 5D)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the number of TMDs in human EMC clients compared to all secretory proteins, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Human EMC clients are more likely to contain charged and aromatic residues distributed throughout the TMD.
source: and, like the yeast clients, are more likely to contain charged and aromatic residues distributed throughout the TMD (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by amino acid composition analysis of TMDs in human EMC clients, shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: GO terms associated with the identified human clients were enriched for transporter related terms which constituted the largest class of proteins whose abundance decreased upon EMC depletion.
source: Further mirroring the yeast EMC client profile, GO terms associated with the identified human clients were enriched for transporter related terms which constituted the largest class of proteins whose abundance decreased upon EMC depletion (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of human EMC clients, shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The predominant function of the EMC is to ensure the biogenesis of a subset of multipass membrane proteins.
source: Our work establishes that the predominant function of the EMC is to ensure the biogenesis of a subset of multipass membrane proteins.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EMC cotranslationally interacts with nascent polypeptides.
source: These studies are consistent with a model in which the EMC cotranslationally interacts with nascent polypeptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-specific ribosome profiling data showing EMC engagement during translation.

claim: Following synthesis, the EMC stabilizes clients and enables recruitment of substrate-specific and general chaperones to achieve a conformation that is competent for function in the ER or for transport to the Golgi.
source: Following synthesis, the EMC stabilizes clients and enables recruitment of substrate-specific and general chaperones to achieve a conformation that is competent for function in the ER or for transport to the Golgi (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is a model based on the observation that EMC interacts with clients, chaperones, and co-chaperones, and that clients are destabilized in EMC-depleted cells.

claim: In the absence of the EMC, newly synthesized client proteins are likely extracted from the membrane for degradation by the UPS.
source: In the absence of the EMC, newly synthesized client proteins are likely extracted from the membrane for degradation by the UPS (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that client proteins are destabilized and degraded in EMC-depleted cells, with speculation about the degradation mechanism.

claim: The EMC directly interacts with and stabilizes a range of client proteins consisting primarily of multipass transmembrane proteins.
source: First, the EMC directly interacts with and stabilizes a range of client proteins consisting primarily of multipass transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown experiments in yeast and proteomics in human cells showing EMC interactions with multipass proteins.

claim: The EMC can begin to interact cotranslationally and subsequently stabilize newly synthesized client proteins, likely preventing premature degradation by ERAD.
source: Second, the EMC can begin to interact cotranslationally and subsequently stabilize newly synthesized client proteins, likely preventing premature degradation by ERAD.
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-specific ribosome profiling data showing cotranslational EMC engagement and proteomics data showing client destabilization in EMC-depleted cells.

claim: The EMC engages transporters and other client proteins enriched for sub-optimal residues in transmembrane helices.
source: Third, the EMC engages transporters and other client proteins enriched for sub-optimal residues in transmembrane helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by amino acid composition analysis of TMDs in EMC clients and gene ontology analysis showing enrichment for transporters.

claim: The EMC typically engages transporters and other membrane proteins enriched for charged residues in TMDs following synthesis of TMD clusters.
source: Our proximity-specific ribosome profiling results indicate that the EMC typically engages transporters and other membrane proteins enriched for charged residues in TMDs (Figure 4 B and C) following synthesis of TMD clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by proximity-specific ribosome profiling data showing EMC engagement following TMD clusters and amino acid composition analysis.

claim: All of the EMC clients identified in yeast are dependent on SRP and are cotranslationally targeted to the ER.
source: In addition, all of the EMC clients identified in yeast are dependent on SRP, a factor that cotranslationally delivers substrates to the ER surface, and are cotranslationally targeted to the ER (Costa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Costa et al., 2018, which characterized the targeting mechanism of EMC clients.

claim: All of the mammalian multipass protein EMC substrates were previously found to be cotranslationally targeted to the ER by proximity-specific ribosome profiling studies.
source: Similarly, all of the mammalian multipass protein EMC substrates were previously found to be cotranslationally targeted to the ER by proximity-specific ribosome profiling studies (Jan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jan et al., 2014, which characterized the targeting mechanism of mammalian EMC clients.

claim: The EMC can engage client proteins cotranslationally, perhaps following insertion via the translocon into the ER membrane, likely acting to stabilize folding intermediates and to forestall degradation.
source: Overall, our results support a model in which the EMC can engage client proteins cotranslationally, perhaps following insertion via the translocon into the ER membrane, likely acting to stabilize folding intermediates and to forestall degradation.
evidence: This claim is a model based on proximity-specific ribosome profiling data and proteomics data, with speculation about the mechanism of EMC action.

claim: The EMC promotes the biogenesis of a wide range of human multipass client proteins by stabilizing transmembrane regions during biosynthesis and prior to completion of folding.
source: Thus, we propose that the EMC promotes the biogenesis of a wide range of human multipass client proteins by stabilizing transmembrane regions during biosynthesis and prior to completion of folding.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on the observation that EMC clients have destabilizing features in TMDs and are destabilized in EMC-depleted cells.

claim: A unifying function of the EMC is to accommodate and stabilize the wide diversity of membrane spanning sequences by directly interacting with select membrane proteins with destabilizing features in TMDs.
source: Therefore, we propose that a unifying function of the EMC is to accommodate and stabilize the wide diversity of membrane spanning sequences by directly interacting with select membrane proteins with destabilizing features in TMDs.
evidence: This claim is a proposed unifying model based on the observation that EMC acts on both multipass proteins and TA proteins with low hydrophobicity.

claim: The TMD of EMC1 was previously shown to bind to and stabilize a destabilized, ER membrane embedded SV40 virion.
source: This property is consistent with the previously reported role for the TMD of EMC1 in binding to and stabilizing a destabilized, ER membrane embedded SV40 virion (Bagchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bagchi et al., 2016, which demonstrated EMC1's role in SV40 virion stabilization.

claim: EMC3 may share a common ancestry with the universally conserved YidC/Oxa1/Alb3 protein family in bacteria and mitochondria.
source: Interestingly, EMC3 may share a common ancestry with the universally conserved YidC/Oxa1/Alb3 protein family in bacteria and mitochondria (Anghel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Anghel et al., 2017, which proposed the evolutionary relationship between EMC3 and YidC/Oxa1/Alb3.

claim: YidC plays a dual role in both the insertion of membrane proteins and the stabilization of membrane proteins inserted via the translocon by direct interaction with SecYEG.
source: YidC also plays a dual role in both the insertion of membrane proteins (Samuelson et al., 2000) and the stabilization of membrane proteins inserted via the translocon by direct interaction with SecYEG (Nagamori et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Samuelson et al., 2000 and Nagamori et al., 2004, which demonstrated YidC's dual role in membrane protein biogenesis.

claim: The EMC recruits substrate-specific chaperones including Ilm1, Sop4 and Gsf2, as well as general cytoplasmic and lumenal chaperones and oxidoreductases.
source: Indeed, we find that in yeast the EMC also recruits substrate-specific chaperones including Ilm1, Sop4 and Gsf2, as well as general cytoplasmic and lumenal chaperones and oxidoreductases.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown experiments showing EMC interactions with these chaperones.

claim: The EMC may hold folding intermediates in a privileged, ERAD-protected state until the recruitment of substrate-specific chaperones and/or general chaperones to complete folding and allow ER export.
source: We propose that, in analogy to the recently described function of the Slp1-Emp65 complex for soluble lumenal ER proteins (Zhang et al., 2017), the EMC may also hold folding intermediates in a privileged, ERAD-protected state until the recruitment of substrate-specific chaperones and/or general chaperones to complete folding and allow ER export.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on the observation that EMC interacts with clients and chaperones, with analogy to the Slp1-Emp65 complex cited from Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: The EMC may compartmentalize multiple functions necessary for membrane protein biogenesis: transmembrane stabilization, recruitment of folding factors and protection of folding intermediates from recognition and degradation by the ER quality control machinery.
source: Thus, the EMC may compartmentalize multiple functions necessary for membrane protein biogenesis: transmembrane stabilization, recruitment of folding factors and protection of folding intermediates from recognition and degradation by the ER quality control machinery.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model summarizing the multiple functions of the EMC based on all the experimental data.

claim: Less than 50% of newly synthesized CFTR folds properly and traffics out of the ER in healthy cells under normal conditions.
source: Even in healthy cells under normal conditions, less than 50% of newly synthesized CFTR folds properly and traffics out of the ER (Kopito, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kopito, 1999, which reported the folding efficiency of CFTR.

claim: The treatment for the most common form of cystic fibrosis (CFTR∆F508) employs a drug combination including a 'folding corrector' to allow increased ER exit and transport to the cell surface and a 'potentiator' to increase chloride transport activity.
source: Indeed, the treatment for the most common form of cystic fibrosis (CFTR∆F508) employs a drug combination including a 'folding corrector' to allow increased ER exit and transport to the cell surface and a 'potentiator' to increase chloride transport activity (Boyle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boyle et al., 2014, which described the therapeutic strategy for cystic fibrosis.

claim: Disease-associated mutations often cluster within transmembrane helices.
source: Disease-associated mutations often cluster within transmembrane helices (Sanders and Myers, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sanders and Myers, 2004, which reported the clustering of disease mutations in TMDs.

claim: Disease-associated mutations are biased towards missense mutations, resulting in the addition of polar or charged residues within transmembrane helices.
source: and are biased towards missense mutations, resulting in the addition of polar or charged residues within transmembrane helices (Partridge et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Partridge et al., 2002, which reported the bias towards missense mutations in TMDs.

claim: Individual transmembrane domains (TMDs) of multipass proteins are cotranslationally inserted into the lipid bilayer, and this step can often be energetically costly.
source: Individual transmembrane domains (TMDs) of multipass proteins are cotranslationally inserted into the lipid bilayer, and this step can often be energetically costly (Cymer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cymer et al., 2015, which discussed the energetics of TMD insertion.

claim: The length of the TMD may not match the thickness of the lipid bilayer in the ER due to differences in membrane composition between the ER and the protein's final destination.
source: First, the length of the TMD may not match the thickness of the lipid bilayer in the ER due to differences in membrane composition between the ER and the protein's final destination (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sharpe et al., 2010, which discussed TMD length mismatch with ER membrane thickness.

claim: Transporters, transmembrane ATPases, and solute carriers contain polar and/or charged residues within membrane spanning domains that form aqueous channels within the plane of the membrane.
source: Transporters, transmembrane ATPases, and solute carriers, for example, contain polar and/or charged residues within membrane spanning domains that form aqueous channels within the plane of the membrane (Tector and Hartl, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tector and Hartl, 1999, which discussed the presence of charged residues in transporter TMDs.

claim: Sop4 is a near-stoichiometric interactor with the EMC, but shares only a subset of the characteristic genetic interactions of other core components.
source: Although Sop4 is a near-stoichiometric interactor with the EMC, it shares only a subset of the characteristic genetic interactions of other core components (Jonikas et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing Sop4 interaction with EMC and a citation to Jonikas et al., 2009 for genetic interaction data.

claim: The full function of the EMC complex does not depend on Sop4, and it may play a role distinct from the core complex.
source: suggesting that, in contrast to the six core EMC components (Emc1-6), the full function of the EMC complex does not depend on Sop4, and it may play a role distinct from the core complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Sop4 has different genetic interactions than core EMC components.

claim: Ilm1 is a poorly characterized ER-localized protein.
source: and Ilm1, a poorly characterized ER-localized protein (Lockshon et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lockshon et al., 2007, which characterized Ilm1 localization.
